name: Apple
benefits: Soluble fibre (pectin) that feeds gut bacteria
Quercetin, an anti-inflammatory antioxidant
Very low energy density, so it fills you up cheaply
warnings: Wash well — apples are among the most pesticide-sprayed crops
Do not chew the seeds in quantity; they contain amygdalin
note: Eat it with the skin on. Most of the fibre and antioxidants sit in the peel.

name: Banana
benefits: High potassium, which helps control blood pressure
Vitamin B6 for nerve and brain function
Resistant starch when slightly green
warnings: Higher sugar than most fruit — diabetics should stick to half a banana
People with kidney disease should watch the potassium load
note: The riper it gets, the faster the sugar hits your blood. A slightly green banana is gentler.

name: Mango
benefits: Enormous vitamin C and vitamin A content
Digestive enzymes (amylases) that help break down starch
Beta-carotene for eye health
warnings: One of the sweetest fruits — go easy if you are diabetic
Artificially ripened mangoes may carry calcium carbide residue
note: Buy naturally ripened fruit. Uniformly yellow skin with no fragrance is a warning sign of chemical ripening.

name: Orange
benefits: A single orange covers a full day of vitamin C
Folate, which matters in pregnancy
Hesperidin, linked to healthier blood vessels
warnings: The acid can wear tooth enamel — rinse with water afterwards
note: Eat the fruit rather than drinking the juice. Juicing throws away the fibre and triples the sugar hit.

name: Grapes
benefits: Resveratrol in the skin, studied for heart health
Good hydration content
Vitamin K for blood clotting
warnings: Very high sugar with very little fibre to slow it down
Heavy pesticide residue — soak in salt water before eating
A choking hazard for small children unless halved
note: Easy to eat an entire bowl without noticing. Portion them out first.

name: Watermelon
benefits: 92% water, excellent for rehydration
Lycopene, an antioxidant linked to heart health
Very low calorie for the volume you get
warnings: High glycaemic index despite the low sugar total
Injected or dyed melons are sold in some markets — an unnaturally red, mushy interior is a red flag
note: One of the safest things you can eat in hot weather. Just buy it whole rather than pre-cut.

name: Dried Dates
benefits: Genuinely high fibre for a sweet food
Iron, potassium and magnesium
A far better sugar source than refined sweets
warnings: 63 g of sugar per 100 g — this is concentrated fruit sugar
Often treated with sulphites, which trigger asthma
Sticky texture clings to teeth and feeds decay
note: Nutritious, but treat it like a sweet rather than like fruit. Two or three is a portion.

safeLimit.note: About two Medjool dates. Enough for the iron and fibre without spending your whole sugar budget.

name: Spinach
benefits: Dense in iron, folate and vitamin K
Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the retina
Nitrates that modestly lower blood pressure
warnings: High in oxalates — a real concern if you form kidney stones
Oxalates also block calcium and iron absorption
Wash thoroughly; leafy greens are a common source of food poisoning
note: Cooking it briefly cuts the oxalate load and makes the iron easier to absorb. Add lemon to help further.

name: Carrot
benefits: Beta-carotene converts to vitamin A for eyesight
Fibre that supports regular digestion
Crunch that satisfies a snack craving for almost no calories
warnings: Eating extreme amounts daily can turn skin orange (carotenemia) — harmless but odd
note: A little oil alongside dramatically improves how much beta-carotene you actually absorb.

name: Broccoli
benefits: Sulforaphane, one of the most studied anti-cancer plant compounds
More vitamin C by weight than an orange
Good protein for a vegetable
warnings: Can cause gas and bloating in sensitive stomachs
Large amounts may interfere with thyroid function if you are iodine deficient
note: Steam it, do not boil it. Boiling leaches out most of the sulforaphane and vitamin C.

name: Potato (Boiled)
benefits: More potassium than a banana
Vitamin C survives boiling reasonably well
Cooled boiled potato forms resistant starch, which feeds gut bacteria
warnings: High glycaemic index — it spikes blood sugar quickly
Green patches and sprouts contain solanine, which is toxic. Cut them away
note: The potato is not the problem. What we usually do to it — deep frying, salting, crisping — is.

name: Tomato
benefits: Lycopene, strongly linked to lower prostate cancer risk
Vitamin C and potassium
Almost no calories
warnings: Acidic — can worsen acid reflux
Nightshade family; a small number of people with arthritis report flare-ups
note: Cooking tomatoes actually increases the lycopene you can absorb, unlike most nutrients.

name: Onion
benefits: Quercetin, an anti-inflammatory antioxidant
Prebiotic fibre that feeds beneficial gut bacteria
Sulphur compounds linked to lower cholesterol
warnings: A common IBS trigger because of its FODMAP content
Raw onion worsens acid reflux in some people
note: Raw onion keeps more of its sulphur compounds than cooked. Slice it and let it sit ten minutes before eating.

name: Potato Chips (Salted)
benefits: Some potassium and fibre survive from the potato
warnings: Deep frying at high heat generates acrylamide, a probable carcinogen
Very high sodium — one pack is a quarter of your daily limit
Engineered salt-fat-crunch combination that makes stopping genuinely hard
note: The single worst thing here is not the fat, it is that a 30 g pack is almost impossible to stop at.

name: Nacho Cheese Tortilla Chips
benefits: Whole corn provides a little fibre
warnings: Contains Sunset Yellow, tied to hyperactivity in children
MSG plus disodium inosinate is a double flavour-enhancer load
700 mg sodium per 100 g
note: The cheese flavour is almost entirely maltodextrin, MSG and colour. There is very little actual cheese.

name: Cheese Corn Puffs
warnings: Two synthetic azo dyes that carry hyperactivity warnings in the EU
900 mg sodium per 100 g, among the saltiest snacks sold
Almost no fibre — it is refined starch, oil, salt and colour
note: Marketed hardest at children, which is exactly the group the colours in it are flagged for.

name: Roasted Salted Peanuts
benefits: 26 g of protein per 100 g
Mostly monounsaturated fat, the heart-friendly kind
High fibre and good magnesium content
warnings: One of the most severe allergens in existence
Added salt pushes sodium up unnecessarily — buy unsalted
Poorly stored peanuts can carry aflatoxin, a liver carcinogen
note: Genuinely good food wrapped in unnecessary salt. Unsalted roasted peanuts score much better.

name: Bhujia / Fried Sev
benefits: Gram flour base gives it real protein and fibre
warnings: 16 g saturated fat per 100 g from palm oil
Repeatedly reused frying oil raises trans fat further
Tartrazine colour is added purely for appearance
note: The gram flour is fine. The palm oil it is fried in, and how often it gets reused, is the problem.

name: Popcorn (Air-popped, Plain)
benefits: A whole grain, with 15 g of fibre per 100 g
Very high volume for very few calories
Polyphenol content comparable to some fruits
warnings: Microwave popcorn is a different food entirely — bag coatings and butter flavouring change the picture
Hulls can lodge in the gums
note: The best snack on this list, provided you pop it yourself and skip the butter and salt.

name: Cola (Regular)
warnings: One can holds about 35 g of sugar — more than a full day's limit
Phosphoric acid is linked to lower bone density and enamel erosion
Liquid sugar does not trigger fullness, so it is added on top of everything else you eat
note: A single can blows past the WHO daily sugar cap. There is no nutritional upside to weigh against it.

name: Diet Cola (Zero Sugar)
benefits: No sugar and effectively no calories
A genuine step down from regular cola if you are switching
warnings: Aspartame was classed as possibly carcinogenic by IARC in 2023
Unsafe for anyone with phenylketonuria
Still acidic enough to erode enamel, and still keeps the sweet-craving cycle going
note: Better than full-sugar cola, but that is a low bar. It is not a health drink.

name: Orange Soft Drink
warnings: Sunset Yellow colour carries an EU hyperactivity warning
Sodium benzoate alongside added vitamin C can form traces of benzene
36 g of sugar per can, with no fruit content worth mentioning
note: Despite the fruit on the label, most orange sodas contain little or no actual juice.

name: Packaged Mango Juice
benefits: Some vitamin C, usually added back after processing
warnings: Most so-called juices are under 20% fruit; the rest is sugar and water
Sulphite preservative is an asthma trigger
All the fibre is stripped out, so the sugar hits fast
note: Check the label for the actual fruit percentage. If it says fruit drink rather than juice, it is mostly sugar water.

name: Energy Drink
benefits: Short-term alertness from the caffeine
warnings: 80 mg or more of caffeine per can, on top of sugar
Linked to heart rhythm disturbances in young people
Genuinely dangerous mixed with alcohol — it masks how drunk you are
Not suitable for children or pregnant women
note: The combination of a big caffeine dose with a big sugar dose is what makes these harder on the heart than coffee.

safeLimit.note: One can maximum for a healthy adult, and none at all for under-18s, pregnant women, or anyone with a heart condition.

name: Tender Coconut Water
benefits: Natural electrolytes — potassium, sodium and magnesium
Genuinely effective rehydration after heat or exercise
Very low sugar compared with any sports drink
warnings: High potassium makes it unsuitable in kidney disease
Bottled versions often have added sugar and preservatives
note: Drink it straight from the coconut. Bottled coconut water is a different and much weaker product.

name: Green Tea (Unsweetened)
benefits: Catechins (EGCG), among the best-studied antioxidants there are
Mild caffeine lift without the crash
Associated with lower cardiovascular risk in long-term studies
warnings: Tannins block iron absorption — do not drink it with meals if you are anaemic
Still contains caffeine, so avoid it late in the evening
note: Brew at about 80 C. Boiling water scorches the leaves and makes it bitter.

name: Whole Milk
benefits: Complete protein with all essential amino acids
Calcium and vitamin D for bone density
Vitamin B12, hard to get outside animal foods
warnings: Around 65% of adults worldwide are lactose intolerant to some degree
One of the most common childhood allergies
Saturated fat adds up if you drink several glasses a day
note: The sugar shown is lactose, which occurs naturally. It does not count toward your added-sugar limit.

name: Plain Curd / Yoghurt
benefits: Live probiotic cultures that support gut health
Easier to digest than milk — fermentation breaks down much of the lactose
Calcium and protein without any additives
warnings: Still a dairy allergen
Set at home or check the label; some commercial curd contains thickeners
note: One of the few dairy products that is better for you than the milk it came from.

name: Fruit Flavoured Yoghurt
benefits: Retains the protein and calcium of plain yoghurt
Some products still carry live cultures
warnings: 14 g of sugar per 100 g — roughly three times plain curd
Carmine colouring is insect-derived and not vegetarian
Real fruit content is usually under 5%
note: Buy plain curd and add your own fruit. You cut the sugar by two thirds and lose nothing.

name: Paneer / Cottage Cheese
benefits: 18 g of protein per 100 g, excellent for vegetarians
Very high calcium
No additives when made fresh
warnings: 13 g saturated fat per 100 g — this is a rich food
Adulteration with starch or detergent is common in loose market paneer
Spoils fast; refrigerate and use within two days
note: Excellent protein, but calorie-dense. A 100 g portion is a serving, not a snack.

name: Processed Cheese Slice
benefits: Decent protein and calcium
Long shelf life
warnings: 1300 mg sodium per 100 g — among the saltiest foods in a normal diet
16 g saturated fat per 100 g
Legally often cannot be called cheese; it is a cheese product with emulsifying salts
note: Two slices in a sandwich is over a quarter of your daily sodium before you add anything else.

name: Butter
benefits: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K2
Butyrate, which supports the gut lining
No additives in plain butter
warnings: 51 g saturated fat per 100 g, the highest on this list
Salted butter adds a surprising amount of sodium
Very easy to over-apply without noticing
note: The small amount of trans fat in butter is ruminant trans fat, which does not behave like the industrial kind, so it is not counted against it here.

name: White Bread
benefits: Usually fortified with B vitamins and iron
Cheap, filling energy
warnings: Refined flour with the bran and germ removed, so most fibre is gone
High glycaemic index — it spikes blood sugar like sugar does
490 mg sodium per 100 g is easy to overlook in a staple
note: Bread is where hidden salt sneaks into most diets, simply because people eat so much of it.

name: Whole Wheat Roti / Chapati
benefits: Whole grain, so the fibre and germ are intact
Slow-release energy with a moderate glycaemic index
No additives or preservatives when made at home
warnings: Not suitable for coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity
Adding ghee or butter on top changes the picture considerably
note: One of the best staples on this list — as long as it is genuine whole wheat atta rather than refined maida.

name: Cream Filled Biscuits
warnings: 32 g sugar per 100 g — a third of the biscuit is sugar
Palm oil pushes saturated fat to 11 g per 100 g
Refined flour, refined sugar and refined fat with almost no fibre
note: The cream filling is sugar and palm oil whipped together. There is no dairy cream in it.

name: Marie / Digestive Biscuit
benefits: Lower sugar than cream biscuits
Some fibre in the wholemeal versions
warnings: Still 20 g sugar per 100 g despite the plain, healthy-looking image
Palm oil is the main fat
The word digestive is marketing, not a health claim
note: Better than a cream biscuit, but it is still a sweet refined-flour snack, not a health food.

name: Frosted Breakfast Cereal
benefits: Fortified with iron and B vitamins
Low in fat
warnings: 36 g sugar per 100 g — over a third of the box is sugar
BHA preservative is listed as a possible human carcinogen
500 mg sodium per 100 g in a food that tastes purely sweet
note: Marketed as a healthy breakfast, but by sugar content it sits closer to a biscuit than to a bowl of oats.

name: Rolled Oats (Plain)
benefits: Beta-glucan fibre, proven to lower LDL cholesterol
16.9 g protein per 100 g, very high for a grain
Slow-release carbohydrate that keeps you full for hours
warnings: Often cross-contaminated with wheat, so check the label if you are coeliac
Flavoured instant oat sachets are a completely different product, loaded with sugar
note: Buy plain oats and sweeten them yourself. The flavoured sachets undo most of the benefit.

name: Egg (Boiled)
benefits: The reference protein against which all others are measured
Choline for brain and liver function
Lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health
warnings: A common childhood allergen
Undercooked eggs carry a salmonella risk
Dietary cholesterol matters less than once thought, but people with familial hypercholesterolaemia should still moderate
note: The old advice to limit eggs to two a week has largely been abandoned. One or two a day is fine for most adults.

name: Chicken Breast (Cooked)
benefits: 31 g of complete protein per 100 g
Very low saturated fat when skinless
Rich in B vitamins, selenium and phosphorus
warnings: Raw chicken is a major salmonella and campylobacter risk — cook to 75 C
Charring it on a grill creates heterocyclic amines, which are carcinogenic
Antibiotic residue is a concern with some intensively farmed poultry
note: One of the cleanest protein sources available. How you cook it decides whether it stays that way.

name: Lentils / Dal (Cooked)
benefits: Protein and fibre in the same package, which is rare
Folate, iron and potassium
Low glycaemic index, so blood sugar stays steady
warnings: Can cause gas and bloating — soaking before cooking helps
Contains lectins and phytates, both largely destroyed by proper cooking
Not a complete protein on its own; pair it with rice or roti
note: Dal with rice or roti gives you a complete amino acid profile, which is why the combination is a staple across so many cultures.

name: Salami / Processed Sausage
benefits: High protein content
warnings: Processed meat is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen — the same confidence category as tobacco smoke
1740 mg sodium per 100 g, close to a full day's limit
Sodium nitrite forms nitrosamines when fried at high heat
note: Group 1 means the evidence that it causes cancer is strong, not that the risk per serving is as large as smoking. Roughly 50 g a day raises colorectal cancer risk by about 18%.

name: Chickpeas (Cooked)
benefits: High fibre and plant protein together
Very filling, which helps with weight control
Good iron, folate and manganese
warnings: FODMAP content can trigger IBS symptoms
Canned versions can carry a lot of added sodium — rinse them
note: Among the most satiating foods measured. A cup keeps you full far longer than the calories suggest.

name: Tofu
benefits: Complete plant protein with all essential amino acids
Isoflavones associated with lower cardiovascular risk
Calcium-set tofu is a strong non-dairy calcium source
warnings: Soy is a major allergen
People on thyroid medication should leave a gap between the two
Flavoured and fried tofu products carry much more sodium and fat
note: The concern about soy and hormones comes largely from rodent studies at doses no human diet reaches.

name: Milk Chocolate
benefits: Some magnesium and iron from the cocoa
Genuine mood benefit, which is worth something
warnings: 52 g sugar per 100 g — over half the bar is sugar
19 g saturated fat per 100 g
Typically only 20 to 30% actual cocoa
note: The cocoa is the good part, and milk chocolate has the least of it. Every step up in cocoa percentage improves the picture.

name: Dark Chocolate (70% Cocoa)
benefits: Flavanols linked to lower blood pressure and better blood vessel function
11 g fibre per 100 g
High magnesium, iron and copper
warnings: Still 24 g saturated fat and 24 g sugar per 100 g
Very calorie dense — 598 kcal per 100 g
Some dark chocolate carries measurable cadmium and lead from the cocoa
note: The genuine health story is real but small, and it applies to two squares a day, not half a bar.

name: Vanilla Ice Cream
benefits: Some calcium and protein from the dairy base
warnings: 21 g sugar per 100 g
Products labelled frozen dessert rather than ice cream use palm oil instead of milk fat
Emulsifier and stabiliser stack is long even in premium brands
note: Check whether the tub says ice cream or frozen dessert. The second means the milk fat has been swapped for vegetable oil.

name: Gummy Candy
warnings: 60 g sugar per 100 g with zero fibre, vitamins or minerals
Contains titanium dioxide, banned across the EU since 2022
Two azo dyes that carry EU hyperactivity warnings
Sticky texture keeps sugar against the teeth for a long time
note: Effectively sugar, gelatin and colour. There is nothing else in it.

name: Gulab Jamun / Jalebi
benefits: Some protein and calcium when made from real khoya
warnings: Deep fried and then soaked in sugar syrup — 45 g sugar per 100 g
Commercial versions are often fried in reused oil, raising trans fat
Synthetic yellow colour is common in shop-bought jalebi
note: A festival food. The problem is not eating it, it is eating it every week.

name: Instant Noodles (Fried)
benefits: Cheap and fast
Usually fortified with a little iron
warnings: One pack carries roughly 40% of a day's sodium
The noodle block is flash-fried in palm oil before drying
MSG and disodium inosinate together make a very heavy flavour-enhancer load
TBHQ preservative keeps the fried oil stable on the shelf
note: Using half the seasoning sachet and adding an egg and vegetables genuinely improves this a lot.

name: Instant Cup Soup
benefits: Warm and filling for very few calories once made up
warnings: 3000 mg sodium per 100 g of powder, one of the highest figures in any food category
Maltodextrin and starch make up most of the bulk
Real vegetable content is minimal
note: Sodium looks alarming per 100 g because it is a dry powder, but one sachet still delivers roughly 450 mg.

name: Frozen French Fries (Fried)
benefits: Some potassium and fibre survive from the potato
warnings: Among the highest acrylamide levels of any common food
Fried twice — once at the factory, once at home
Sulphite treatment to stop browning is an asthma trigger
note: Air frying instead of deep frying cuts both the fat and the acrylamide substantially. Aim for golden, not brown.

name: Frozen Chicken Nuggets
benefits: Reasonable protein content
warnings: Often made from mechanically separated meat rather than whole cuts
Batter and frying oil account for most of the calories
560 mg sodium per 100 g
note: The protein figure looks respectable, but roughly half the product by weight is batter, oil and water.

name: Tomato Ketchup
benefits: Cooked tomato means the lycopene is well absorbed
warnings: 21 g sugar per 100 g — roughly a quarter of the bottle is sugar
900 mg sodium per 100 g
Sodium benzoate preservative in most brands
note: A tablespoon carries about 4 g of sugar. Nobody stops at a tablespoon, which is where the problem starts.

name: Mayonnaise
benefits: Vitamin E from the vegetable oil base
warnings: 75 g fat per 100 g — the most calorie dense item on this list
Raw egg versions carry a salmonella risk if unrefrigerated
Very easy to add 200 calories to a sandwich without noticing
note: Almost pure oil held in suspension. Treat a tablespoon as a serving, because that alone is 100 calories.

name: Soy Sauce
benefits: Naturally brewed versions contain some beneficial fermentation compounds
warnings: 5490 mg sodium per 100 ml — by far the saltiest thing in this database
Chemically hydrolysed versions can contain 3-MCPD, a possible carcinogen
Contains wheat, so it is not gluten free despite the name
note: Used a teaspoon at a time it is fine. The sodium figure only becomes dangerous when you pour it.

name: Peanut Butter (Natural)
benefits: 25 g protein per 100 g
Mostly monounsaturated fat
Good fibre, magnesium and vitamin E
warnings: Severe allergen
Very calorie dense — easy to eat 400 calories from a jar
Cheaper brands add palm oil and sugar, which changes it completely
note: Buy the kind whose ingredient list reads peanuts, and maybe salt. The oil separating on top is a good sign, not a bad one.

name: Chocolate Hazelnut Spread
benefits: Some hazelnut content contributes vitamin E
warnings: 56 g sugar per 100 g — sugar is the first ingredient, ahead of hazelnuts
Palm oil is the second ingredient
Marketed for breakfast despite being closer to icing than to a spread
note: By weight it is over half sugar and roughly a fifth palm oil. Hazelnuts are about 13%.

name: Mango Pickle (Oil Based)
benefits: Traditionally fermented pickles carry some probiotic bacteria
Spices contribute antioxidants
warnings: 3500 mg sodium per 100 g — salt is the preservation method
High oil content on top of the salt
Sulphite preservative in commercial jars is an asthma trigger
note: A teaspoon alongside a meal is the traditional portion, and at that amount it is fine. It was never meant to be eaten by the spoonful.
